strengths: Fills a genuine gap: there is no established, reference-based benchmark for LFQA evaluation metrics, and CALF is the first systematic attempt with expert-written references from authoritative examination sources.

Well-motivated design choices: six diverse subjects (history, politics, geography, law, medicine, psychology), three comparison settings (human vs. human, human vs. model, model vs. model), and seven question types increase coverage and difficulty diversity.

Careful and transparent annotation pipeline: a structured multi-step recipe (identify key information, check responses, handle correctness levels, compare overlap), two independent annotators with a third meta-reviewer for disagreements, and reported inter-annotator agreement per domain and setting.

Comprehensive evaluation: 7 traditional metrics, 6 prompt-based LLM configurations (including CoT and G-Eval), 3 trained metrics, ICL variants, and two agent systems (ChatEval, ReFeR), plus analyses of metric-to-metric agreement, length bias, and agreement with human consensus.

Useful negative findings with analysis: no metric approaches human performance; CoT, majority voting, ICL, and agent pipelines give limited or no gains; error analysis (Figures 12-13, Appendix C.5) gives concrete examples of why traditional vs. LLM-based metrics fail differently.
Strong reproducibility support: released dataset and code, detailed prompts (Appendix C.7), annotation guidelines, and case studies in the appendix.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on GPT-4o in benchmark construction introduces circularity concerns: references are expanded by GPT-4o and the entire dataset is machine-translated to English by GPT-4o, yet GPT-4o is also one of the evaluated metrics; the gold-standard quality depends on the same model family being tested.

Translation to English with GPT-4o (temperature 1.0) may introduce semantic drift and errors, and results are reported only for translated English text; performance on the original Chinese data is not validated, weakening claims about the benchmark's fidelity.

Inter-annotator agreement is moderate, not above 90% (0.68-0.87), and notably low in some cells (e.g., geography model vs. model at 0.68); this limits the reliability of gold labels for fine-grained distinctions, especially given the benchmark's difficulty claim.

Some methodological choices are ad hoc: rounding traditional metric outputs to two decimal places to induce 'tie' options is crude and may distort metric comparisons; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are reported for the accuracy differences across metrics.

Internal inconsistencies reduce polish: the abstract says 'up to 1476 examples' while the conclusion says '1,500 records'; Table 2 shows N/A for human annotation of law/medicine/psychology but the paper elsewhere describes annotation of model pairs in these domains; Figure 2 and Figure 9 contain typos ('Huamn', 'one in vote').

The annotation criterion is centered on key-information overlap with the reference, which structurally favors reference-based metrics and may disadvantage legitimately different but high-quality answers; the 'totally/partially/totally wrong' handling is subjective and its scoring weights are not formalized.
Only five annotators whose domain expertise is described loosely ('have taken relevant courses'), which raises questions about expert-level reliability in specialized domains like law and medicine.

Positioning relative to the closest prior work (Xu et al., 2023) is somewhat incremental: the contribution is essentially a larger, multi-domain version of an existing pairwise evaluation protocol rather than a new evaluation methodology; the paper provides no new metric, only a diagnosis.

strengths: The paper addresses a real gap: there are few reference-based benchmarks with expert-written references for evaluating LFQA automatic metrics, and sourcing questions/references from Chinese examinations (rather than crowd-sourced ELI5 data) is a reasonable way to obtain authoritative reference answers.

The evaluation is broad in coverage: 7 traditional metrics, prompt-based LLM evaluators (with CoT and G-Eval), trained metrics (Auto-J, TIGERScore, CritiqueLLM), and two agent systems, across three comparison modes (human vs. human, human vs. model, model vs. model) and six subjects.

The paper goes beyond reporting scores, providing inter-annotator agreement, correlation analyses between metrics, agreement analysis on human-disagreement cases, and qualitative error analyses of why ROUGE-style and LLM-based metrics fail.

Positioning against prior work (Krishna et al. 2021, Xu et al. 2023) is clearly articulated, and the data construction pipeline (OCR, manual correction, annotation recipe, tie option, position balancing) is described in reasonable detail with appendices.
weaknesses: The gold standard is noisy, which undermines the paper's central claim that 'no metric matches humans.' Inter-annotator agreement is only 0.68–0.87 and explicitly never exceeds 90%. With a substantial fraction of noisy labels, accuracies below 65% cannot be cleanly attributed to metric failure; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are provided, so most comparisons (e.g., CoT vs. vanilla, GPT-4o vs. GPT-3.5) are within noise.

The reference answers—the core of the benchmark—were rewritten by GPT-4o to be 'more natural.' This makes an LLM a co-author of the evaluation gold standard, and the quality control is thin: only 100 sampled examples were audited (Table 6 reports just 1 error in 600 annotations, which is surprisingly clean and warrants more scrutiny). The circularity of using GPT-4o to transform references while also testing GPT-4o as an evaluator is not discussed.

The data provenance chain is convoluted: Chinese exam questions (sometimes image-based, OCR-extracted), GPT-4o-translated into English so that 'some models cannot achieve comparable results in Chinese.' The benchmark is thus several lossy transformations away from its authoritative source, and translation/OCR errors could materially affect metric judgments. No analysis quantifies error propagation through this pipeline.

Model-generated responses come only from Llama-3-8B and GPT-3.5-turbo with temperature 1.0, and 'difficulty' was engineered by selecting models of similar leaderboard rank. This yields many near-tie pairs (motivating the odd 'tie' option), and the use of only two outdated generators limits the benchmark's coverage of modern model behavior.

Forcing traditional metrics into a triple-choice format by rounding scores to two decimal places is an ad-hoc protocol; the resulting 'tie' rate distribution and its impact on the comparison against LLM evaluators (which can natively output 'tie') are not analyzed.

Novelty is incremental: the task formulation, annotation criteria ('factuality, completeness, clarity'), and metric suite closely follow Xu et al. (2023); the main deltas are the exam-sourced data and larger scale (~1476 examples, which is still modest). The agent/ICL experiments are negative results with limited depth of analysis.

Inconsistencies and sloppiness reduce confidence: the abstract says 1476 examples while the conclusion says 1500; Table 2's caption contradicts the text about which domains have human answers; there are multiple typos ('Huamn,' 'I perfer'); Figure 2 axes are unlabeled.

Scope is narrow (social-science exam-style questions, mostly Chinese education context), limiting generalization of the conclusion that all automatic LFQA metrics are inadequate; the authors themselves defer natural sciences and math to future work.

Reproducibility and legal clarity of the data are questionable: exam papers and student answers from online marking platforms may carry licensing/redistribution restrictions; the paper does not discuss consent or licensing for student-written responses.

strengths: Introduces a new reference-based benchmark (CALF) for LFQA evaluation, addressing a genuine gap: prior evaluation studies (e.g., Xu et al. 2023) relied on small, Reddit/ELI5-derived data without expert-written references.

Sources questions and references from authoritative Chinese examination materials (CEESQ/PEEQ) across six subjects, providing knowledge-intensive, expert-crafted references and a useful taxonomy of seven question types.

Comprehensive experimental coverage: 7 traditional metrics, prompt-based LLM evaluators (GPT-3.5/GPT-4o, CoT, G-Eval), trained metrics (Auto-J, TIGERScore, CritiqueLLM), and two agent systems (ChatEval, ReFeR), giving a fairly complete snapshot of the current evaluation landscape.

Careful human annotation protocol: dual independent annotation with a third annotator for disagreements, reported inter-annotator agreement (Table 2), detailed annotation recipes, and case studies; validation of GPT-4o reference transformation via sampled human audit (Table 6).

Useful analyses beyond headline numbers: agreement between metrics (correlation heatmaps), length bias analysis, comparison of scenarios where humans agree vs. disagree, tie/no-tie ablation, and qualitative error analysis explaining why traditional vs. LLM metrics fail.
Timely and actionable takeaway that neither traditional nor LLM-based metrics (nor agent pipelines) reach human parity on LFQA evaluation, motivating future metric development.
weaknesses: Potential circularity/noise in data construction: references are expanded by GPT-4o and the dataset is translated to English by GPT-4o, so gold references embed LLM artifacts; this could systematically advantage or disadvantage certain metrics, and the human audit covers only 100 sampled examples.

Moderate scale and imbalance: 1476 examples with 96-100 examples per domain for law/psychology/medicine, and those three domains lack human-written responses (model-vs-model only), limiting generality of conclusions for human-vs-model comparisons.

Gold labels rest on 5 annotators (including CS students) whose domain expertise in law/medicine/psychology is asserted but not rigorously credentialed; inter-annotator agreement is only ~0.68-0.87, and no statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are reported for the metric comparisons.

Metric comparison methodology is crude in places: rounding traditional metric outputs to two decimals to induce 'tie' options is ad hoc, and the primary metric (preference matching rate) with a tie option can mask real discrimination ability; results in Table 3 hover around 0.47-0.56, so small measurement noise could affect conclusions.

Model responses are generated only by Llama-3-8B and GPT-3.5-turbo at temperature 1.0 with deliberately similar LMSYS rankings; stronger, more current models are absent, which may limit the benchmark's difficulty spectrum and relevance.

The central finding (no automatic metric matches humans on LFQA) is somewhat expected given prior work (Xu et al. 2023); the contribution is primarily a resource plus confirmation, with limited new insight into how to fix the identified failure modes.

Several presentation issues: inconsistent counts (1476 vs 'up to 1500'), typos ('Huamn vs. Human', 'I perfer'), and reliance on appendices for key analyses (error analysis, detailed results) weakens the main narrative.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and underexplored gap: existing LFQA evaluation benchmarks (e.g., Xu et al. 2023) lack expert-written references, are small (~260 examples), and lack tie options; LFQA-E substantially improves scale (1618 questions, 7323 comparisons), adds multilinguality (English and Chinese), and covers 15 topics across three comparison settings (h v h, h v m, m v m).

Careful data curation with attention to contamination: questions sourced from offline exam papers (CEESQ/PEEQ) and recent Reddit/ELI5 posts, with perplexity and n-gram overlap analyses (Sec 5.5) to support non-contamination claims.

Comprehensive evaluation spanning 17 methods across five categories (static metrics, LLMs, LRMs, reward models, evaluation-specialized models), including recent models (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1, o1-mini, RM-R1), providing a useful reference point for the community.

Thorough analyses beyond the main leaderboard: temperature sensitivity, tie-handling behavior, per-setting generalization (model-vs-model drops up to 14.2%), error taxonomy for LLM judges with case studies, inter-metric Cohen's kappa disagreement, cross-benchmark comparisons, and a TTRL-based improvement experiment giving actionable insights.

Reasonable human annotation protocol: expert annotators, triple-choice format with tie option, independent double annotation, reported Cohen's kappa, and a human baseline re-annotated by doctorate-level annotators.
Reproducibility materials appear extensive (prompts, annotation recipes, cost/time analysis in appendices), and the benchmark/code are stated to be released.
weaknesses: Internal inconsistencies undermine polish and trust: the abstract/intro report 1618 questions and 7323 comparisons while the conclusion states 1625 questions and 7649 comparisons; annotator counts and roles shift between sections; the paper claims 'expert-annotated references' yet LFQA-E-EN references are simply top-ranked Reddit answers.

Reference quality for the English subset is a validity concern: top-voted Reddit answers are used as authoritative references, and the evaluation criterion is essentially reference-overlap ('closer to the reference in terms of content'), which may bias against correct responses that diverge from a single Reddit answer; the annotation criteria focus on factuality/completeness 'according to the reference' rather than ground truth.

Model responses are generated only by weak models (Llama-3-8B-Instruct and GPT-3.5-turbo) deliberately chosen for confusability, which limits the benchmark's coverage of realistic modern deployment scenarios where strong model responses dominate; only two languages are covered despite the 'multilingual' claim.

Some key methodological choices are under-justified: temperature=1.0 for judge models (shown in Sec 5.1 to materially change results and cause LRM collapse), rounding scalar reward outputs to 3 decimals for tie detection, and a 90% consistency qualification threshold on only 35 pre-annotation records.

The headline claim 'no metric performs comparably to human judgment' is supported, but the analysis of why is partly anecdotal (error taxonomy from a small number of case studies on two models); quantitative breakdown of error types and statistical significance tests for the metric comparisons are missing.

Novelty is moderate: the paper is largely a careful extension of Xu et al. (2023) with more data, languages, and newer metrics; the TTRL application is a straightforward adaptation of existing work rather than a methodological contribution.

Several claims need better support: the assertion that RM underperformance stems from 'renouncing the tie option' is speculative; the perplexity-based contamination analysis for the Chinese subset shows a potentially concerning pattern (PPL 7.21, higher n-gram overlap) that is waved off as 'within acceptable bounds' without a clear threshold justification.

strengths: The benchmark is substantially larger than prior expert-annotated LFQA evaluation work (1618 questions / 7323 comparisons vs. ~260 in Xu et al. 2023), spans 15 topics and two languages, and adds a ternary (tie) judgment format that better reflects real comparison scenarios.
The paper covers a broad and reasonably current set of metric families (static metrics, LLM judges, LRMs, reward models, and evaluation-tuned models), which is useful for the community.
The authors provide annotation recipes, prompts, contamination analysis, cost/time analysis, and per-domain breakdowns in the appendix, which helps reproducibility and transparency.
Some analyses are practically informative, e.g., the observation that RM-based metrics generalize poorly and that LRMs collapse under deterministic decoding.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the paper is essentially a scaled-up, multilingual extension of Xu et al. (2023) with references added. The core methodology (pairwise expert comparison against references, metric-human alignment) is inherited, and the paper does not propose a fundamentally new evaluation approach or insight beyond 'metrics are still bad at LFQA'.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence: the abstract reports 1618 questions and 7323 comparisons, while the conclusion reports 1625 questions and 7649 comparisons; topic counts differ across sections (15 topics vs. 9+6). These discrepancies suggest rushed preparation and unclear dataset construction bookkeeping.

Data quality concerns: for the English subset, references are taken from top-voted Reddit answers (with GPT-4o paraphrasing) rather than written by experts, so the claimed 'expert-annotated references' guarantee only applies to part of the data. Reddit upvotes are a weak proxy for factual accuracy in long-form answers. The Chinese human responses are extracted via OCR with unclear error handling.

Annotation reliability and fairness: annotators are paid $2 per question containing 4-6 comparisons, each taking ~7 minutes, which is very low compensation for expert-level annotation and raises questions about annotation quality and ethics. Inter-annotator agreement (kappa ~0.65) is reported only post hoc, and the human baseline uses only 3 annotators on an unspecified subset.

Evaluation protocol choices are questionable: setting temperature to 1.0 for evaluation metrics (encouraging 'diversity' in a judging task) is unusual, and the dramatic LRM collapse at temperature 0 (e.g., o1-mini dropping to 5.8% accuracy on zh) suggests the evaluation is unstable and results may be artifacts of decoding choices rather than meaningful findings. No statistical significance testing is provided for any comparisons.

The tie handling for RM-based metrics (rounding scalar outputs, adding tie options post hoc) disadvantages these baselines in ways that are not carefully justified; the observed 'RM failure' may partially be an artifact of the protocol.

The TTRL/reinforcement learning section (5.7) feels disconnected from the main benchmark contribution: it trains on the same benchmark being evaluated (LFQA-E), conflating benchmark usage with improvement claims, and the analysis of rapid convergence/overfitting is superficial.
Contamination analysis is weak: perplexity and n-gram overlap on two small models is not convincing evidence of non-contamination, especially for CEESQ/PEEQ exam content and recent Reddit data.

Error analysis (Section 5.3) is largely qualitative with ad hoc error taxonomies, no inter-annotator validation of the error labels, and no quantitative rigor; the failure-mode conclusions are stated with more confidence than the evidence supports.
Writing quality is below the bar for a top venue, with grammatical errors, inconsistent terminology (e.g., '17 methods' vs. what is listed), and tables referenced but hard to reconcile with the text.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing LFQA evaluation benchmarks (e.g., Xu et al. 2023) lack expert-written references, are small (~260 examples), English-only, and lack a tie option; LFQA-E provides ~6x more questions, ~28x more pairwise comparisons, expert-annotated references, a three-way (A/B/tie) annotation scheme, and both English and Chinese subsets, which is a meaningful extension.

Careful, mostly well-documented data construction: source data from offline exam papers (CEESQ/PEEQ) and recent Reddit/ELI5 posts to reduce contamination, with explicit contamination checks (perplexity and n-gram overlap, Sec 5.5), LLM-based question filtering validated at 97% accuracy, and reported inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa 0.78 for reference validity, ~0.65 for comparisons).

Broad and well-organized evaluation covering 5 categories of metrics (static, LLM-based, RM-based, LRM-based, evaluation-specific trained models) across three comparison settings (h v h, h v m, m v m), plus useful ablations on temperature, prompt design, tie-exclusion, per-domain performance, cost/latency tradeoffs, and agreement (Cohen's kappa matrices).

Actionable analysis beyond leaderboard reporting: error taxonomy for LLM judges (point identification, irrelevant/incorrect information, contradiction, formatting), demonstration that metrics collapse on m v m settings and on tie decisions, and a practical TTRL-based improvement showing evaluation models can be trained toward human preferences.
Thorough appendix with prompts, annotation recipes, case studies, and per-topic breakdowns supporting reproducibility; code and data availability stated.
weaknesses: Internal inconsistencies that undermine confidence in the reported statistics: the abstract and Table 1 state 1618 questions / 7323 comparisons while the conclusion states 1625 questions / 7649 comparisons; the abstract claims 17 metric methods while the conclusion claims 15; the main results only show a subset of models with the rest deferred to the appendix. These should be reconciled.

Label noise limits the benchmark's authority as ground truth: human baseline accuracy is only ~80% and inter-annotator agreement on comparisons is ~0.65 kappa; with near-random performance by many metrics (40-60% accuracy), the gap between metric and human quality may partly reflect annotation ambiguity rather than metric failure. Error bars or significance tests over comparisons are absent.

Potential circularity/quality concerns in English references: top-ranked Reddit/ELI5 answers are used as 'expert reference' answers, and GPT-4o is used to paraphrase/clean human responses; although validated on 100 samples, this introduces a model-in-the-loop bias into an expert-annotated benchmark, and the validity-check kappa (0.78) only measures whether references are 'valid', not whether they are factually complete or correct.

Novelty is incremental relative to Xu et al. (2023): the core contribution is scaling, multilinguality, and adding references/ties to an existing pairwise-alignment evaluation paradigm; the TTRL experiment is a preliminary application of an existing method rather than a methodological contribution.

Some evaluation protocol choices are questionable and could affect conclusions: temperature=1.0 as the default for LLM judges (with LRMs collapsing at temperature 0), scalar RM scores forced into a three-way decision by an ad-hoc rounding rule, and no discussion of position bias or self-preference bias in LLM-as-judge settings, which are well-known confounds for pairwise comparison benchmarks.

Writing and presentation need polishing: several grammatical issues, figures with small/unreadable axis labels (Figure 2), and unclear notation (e.g., 'de dropped', 'GPT-4o with temperature=0.7 to filter' vs. claimed determinism).
